title: Japan's Spacecraft Heads Off to Grab Pieces of a Mars Moon
summary:
Japan's space agency, JAXA, planned to launch a mission to Phobos on Monday. Phobos is one of the two moons of Mars. People could watch the launch live online.

The mission is called MMX. Its job is to collect bits of Phobos and bring them back to Earth. Scientists want to learn how the moons of Mars were made. Some think they were once asteroids. Others think they formed from leftover space material long ago.

An American astronomer named Asaph Hall found Phobos and the smaller moon, Deimos, in 1877. Phobos means "fear" in ancient Greek, and Deimos means "dread."

NASA helped by giving instruments and technology.

The spacecraft was set to blast off on an H3 rocket from Japan at 3:41 p.m. Eastern time on October 19. It is a long trip. MMX should reach Phobos in August 2027. The samples will not come back to Earth until at least 2031.
why_it_matters: Space rocks brought home can help us learn how our neighborhood in space formed, and today's students could study them one day.
